title: Your Complete Guide to a Faster LASIK Recovery

html:
The good news? LASIK surgery has up to a 99% success rate according to studies cited by the Refractive Surgery Council. And most people notice improved vision within a day of the procedure.

Better yet, a few simple precautions can make recovery more comfortable. From using prescribed eye drops to knowing when you can return to work, exercise, and your usual routine, understanding what to expect helps you protect your results.

Our award-winning team of specialists at Marano Eye Care, a division of Ophthalmology New Jersey, has the medical expertise you need to ensure success for complex surgeries like LASIK. We’re also committed to enlisting your informed involvement in aftercare.

Here’s how to support healing, minimize irritation, and give your eyes the best possible start after LASIK.

What to expect after LASIK

One of LASIK's biggest advantages is its relatively short recovery period. Many patients experience clearer vision within 24 hours. However, temporary blurriness, light sensitivity, watery eyes, or a gritty sensation are common early on, and vision can fluctuate slightly as your eyes heal.

Your surgeon provides specific expectations and instructions based on your procedure and individual needs. Following that guidance is the foundation of a smooth LASIK recovery.

Follow your eye drop schedule

Eye drops can play an important role in protecting your eyes after LASIK. Your surgeon may prescribe antibiotic and anti-inflammatory drops to reduce infection risk and control inflammation.

Use each medication exactly as directed, even if your eyes feel comfortable. If you’re unsure about the timing or order of your drops, ask your surgical team rather than guessing.

Preservative-free artificial tears may help with dryness, especially if you need frequent lubrication, but only if your surgeon recommends them.

Avoid rubbing your eyes when they feel dry or itchy. Rubbing can interfere with healing and potentially displace the corneal flap.

Protect your eyes

Your eyes may feel better surprisingly quickly, but that doesn't mean they're fully healed. Take extra care, especially during the first several days.

Wear any protective eye shields provided by your surgeon, particularly while sleeping, for as long as instructed. They help prevent accidental rubbing or pressure on your eyes.

Keep water, soap, shampoo, and other potential irritants out of your eyes, and avoid dusty or smoky environments when possible.

Sunglasses can make bright outdoor conditions more comfortable and help reduce light sensitivity. Otherwise, follow your surgeon's instructions for protecting your eyes outdoors.

Return to your routine gradually as directed

Rest on the day of surgery and give yourself time to adjust before resuming normal activities. Many people return to desk work within a day or two, depending on their vision, comfort, and job requirements.

Light walking is often acceptable soon after surgery, but you may need to wait on strenuous exercise, swimming, contact sports, and activities that expose your eyes to dirt or impact. Your surgeon will tell you when it’s safe to resume them.

Avoid eye makeup until your surgeon says you can use it again. Don't drive until your vision meets legal requirements and your surgeon confirms it’s safe.

Keep every follow-up appointment

Even when your vision seems excellent, follow-up visits matter. Your Marano Eye Care surgeon checks how your eyes are healing, evaluates your vision, and looks for signs of complications or persistent dryness.

Between visits, seek prompt medical attention if you develop severe or worsening eye pain, a sudden decline in vision, increasing redness, or symptoms that seem to be getting worse rather than better. These changes should not be dismissed as routine recovery.

Give your eyes time to heal

With the right care and realistic expectations, you can support healing and enjoy clearer vision with greater confidence.

title: Thinking About Ditching Contacts? Here's What to Know Before LASIK
desc: LASIK has helped millions of people reduce or eliminate their dependence on glasses and contacts. Like any surgery, taking the right steps before the procedure
html:
If you’ve spent years cleaning contacts, buying solution, or waking up wondering whether you accidentally slept in your lenses, tossing them aside after LASIK can feel like a huge relief.

Our specialists at Marano Eye Care, a division of Ophthalmology New Jersey, would be happy to celebrate that victory with you. We specialize in advanced eye care for the entire family, including intricate surgeries like LASIK. Our team enjoys sharing our expertise with our neighbors in Denville, Livingston, and Newark, New Jersey.

But before you decide to ditch your contacts for good, there are several things worth knowing about the procedure and the evaluation that must come first.

LASIK reshapes the cornea

LASIK, short for laser-assisted in situ keratomileusis, corrects certain types of refractive errors by changing the shape of the cornea, the clear surface at the front of the eye.

During the procedure, we use a laser to remove precisely calculated amounts of corneal tissue so light can focus more accurately on the retina. The procedure is generally quick, and numbing eye drops keep you comfortable throughout.

However, because LASIK changes the cornea's structure, careful measurements and screening are essential before treatment.

Not everyone is a candidate

Having a prescription for glasses or contacts does not automatically make someone a good LASIK candidate.

During a consultation, your Marano Eye Care surgeon evaluates your prescription, corneal thickness and shape, tear-film health, and overall eye health. Certain conditions, including some corneal disorders, uncontrolled dry eye, and autoimmune diseases, may affect whether LASIK is advisable.

Your prescription also needs to be reasonably stable. If your vision has changed significantly recently, your doctor may recommend waiting before considering surgery.

The evaluation is about more than checking whether you can read the smallest line on an eye chart. The goal is to determine whether your eyes are healthy enough for the procedure and whether LASIK is likely to provide a useful improvement.

You need to take a preoperative break from contacts

This can be an easy detail to overlook when you're eager to move forward.

Contact lenses can temporarily alter the cornea's shape, which may affect the measurements used to plan LASIK. For that reason, your eye doctor may ask you to stop wearing contacts for a period of time before your evaluation and then again before surgery.

How long you need to go without contacts depends partly on the type of lenses you wear and how frequently you use them. Follow your surgeon's specific instructions rather than switching back to contacts on your own schedule.

Understand what LASIK can and can’t do

One of the most important parts of a LASIK consultation is discussing expectations.

LASIK can reduce dependence on glasses and contact lenses, but it doesn't guarantee you will never need corrective lenses again. Some people may still use glasses for certain activities such as reading.

And as you get older, the natural lens inside the eye gradually becomes less able to focus on nearby objects. This age-related change, called presbyopia, can occur even after successful LASIK.

In other words, LASIK corrects your current refractive error; it does not stop the eyes’ normal aging process.

Understanding LASIK recovery 

Many people notice improved vision relatively soon after LASIK, although the experience varies from person to person. Temporary symptoms such as dry eyes, fluctuating vision, glare, halos, or increased sensitivity to light can occur during healing.

Your surgeon will provide instructions for using prescribed eye drops and protecting your eyes while they recover. Follow-up appointments are also important, even if your vision seems excellent.

Want to know more about LASIK?

If you're tired of glasses and contacts, LASIK may be a life-altering option, but the right starting point is a comprehensive evaluation, not simply choosing a procedure date.

title: All-Laser LASIK vs. Traditional LASIK: What Sets Them Apart?
desc: Considering LASIK but confused about the different types available? Check the basics about two LASIK techniques, including how they work and which one offers th
html:
For many people tired of reaching for glasses or contact lenses every morning, LASIK can seem like a simple path to clearer vision.

But once you start researching the procedure, you may come across terms such as “all-laser LASIK,” “bladeless LASIK,” and “traditional LASIK.” What do these names actually mean?

Although both approaches use a laser to reshape the cornea and correct refractive errors, they differ in how the surgeon creates the corneal flap. Understanding that distinction can make your consultation more informative and help you feel more confident about your options.

Our team at Marano Eye Care, a division of Ophthalmology New Jersey, always encourages our patients to explore their diagnostic and treatment options regarding vision. We’re happy to cover the basics of the two most common types of LASIK here.

Traditional LASIK

Traditional LASIK generally involves two main steps. First, the surgeon creates a thin flap in the cornea using a mechanical instrument called a microkeratome. The flap is then gently lifted, exposing the underlying tissue.

Next, your surgeon uses an excimer laser to remove microscopic amounts of tissue to reshape the cornea. This changes how light enters the eye, helping correct common refractive errors such as nearsightedness (myopia), farsightedness (hyperopia), and astigmatism.

Once the reshaping is complete, the surgeon repositions the corneal flap, where it naturally begins to adhere as the eye heals.

Despite the word “traditional,” this approach remains an established and widely performed type of LASIK.

The all-laser LASIK difference

The biggest distinction in these LASIK approaches is how we create the corneal flap. With all-laser LASIK, sometimes called bladeless LASIK, your surgeon uses a femtosecond laser to create the flap instead of a mechanical microkeratome.

The rest of the procedure is similar to other types of LASIK. After the flap is lifted, we use an excimer laser to precisely reshape the corneal tissue according to your prescription and treatment plan.

Using a laser for flap creation allows our surgeons to program specific flap dimensions, including its depth, diameter, and configuration. That level of control is one reason we favor the all-laser approach.

Does one provide better vision?

Both techniques can provide excellent visual outcomes in appropriately selected patients. However, the quality of the result depends on much more than the instrument used to create the flap.

Factors such as corneal thickness and shape, prescription, eye health, tear-film stability, age, and the specific laser technology used matter. At Marano Eye Care, we consider a thorough preoperative evaluation essential for determining whether LASIK is appropriate in the first place.

Our commitment to providing you with the best option available means we consider your unique visual needs before recommending any procedure.

Recovery and comfort

Both types of LASIK are performed on an outpatient basis, and many patients notice substantially clearer vision soon after surgery. Temporary dryness, light sensitivity, fluctuating vision, or mild discomfort can occur during the early healing period.

Because individual recovery varies, patients should follow their surgeon’s instructions carefully, including recommendations regarding eye drops, avoiding eye rubbing, swimming, and other activities.

Want more information about LASIK and whether it’s right for you?

title: 5 Questions to Ask Your Eye Surgeon Before Scheduling LASIK
desc: Deciding to have LASIK is an exciting step toward reducing your dependence on glasses or contact lenses. However, choosing the right surgeon is just as importan
html:
Laser‑assisted in situ keratomileusis (LASIK) has helped millions of people achieve clearer vision. However, every patient's eyes, lifestyle, and goals are unique. A thoughtful consultation gives you the opportunity to learn whether you're a good candidate and to understand what your results may realistically look like.

We certainly agree with that approach here at Marano Eye Care, a division of Ophthalmology New Jersey. Our team feels that asking the right questions before scheduling surgery can help you feel confident, informed, and prepared to move forward with your vision correction journey.

Here are five questions to get you started.

1. Am I a good candidate for LASIK?

The first question to ask is whether LASIK is truly the best option for your eyes. Not everyone who wants LASIK is an ideal candidate, and our eye surgeons at Marano Eye Care will perform a thorough evaluation before making a recommendation.

We will assess factors such as:

  • Your current prescription and whether it has remained stable
  • Corneal thickness and shape
  • Tear production and overall eye health
  • Your age and medical history
  • Any existing eye conditions, such as cataracts, glaucoma, or keratoconus

If LASIK isn’t the right fit, we offer alternatives that may provide excellent vision correction. Procedures such as photorefractive keratectomy (PRK) or implantable contact lenses (ICLs) may be better suited for certain patients.

2. What technology do you use?

LASIK technology has advanced significantly over the past two decades. Modern diagnostic equipment and laser systems allow our surgeons to customize treatment based on the unique characteristics of each eye.

Ask your surgeon:

  • Is the procedure customized for each patient?
  • Do you use wavefront-guided or topography-guided technology?
  • How do you map the cornea before surgery?
  • What safety features are built into your laser system?

We invest in advanced technology because it often provides more personalized treatment planning and precise outcomes. While no technology can guarantee perfect vision, modern laser platforms help maximize accuracy while enhancing patient safety.

3. What results can I realistically expect?

Every patient hopes for outstanding vision after LASIK, but realistic expectations are essential. Rather than asking whether you'll have "perfect" vision, ask what results someone with your prescription and eye health can reasonably expect.

Expect your Marano Eye Care surgeon to discuss:

  • Your likelihood of achieving 20/20 vision or better
  • Whether you may still need reading glasses later in life
  • The possibility of enhancement procedures if your vision changes
  • Temporary side effects such as glare, halos, or dry eyes during healing

A trustworthy surgeon focuses on education instead of making promises. Understanding both the benefits and limitations of LASIK helps you make an informed decision.

4. What is recovery like?

One of LASIK's biggest advantages is its relatively quick recovery. Many patients notice improved vision within a day, although complete healing continues over several weeks or months.

Ask your surgeon what you should expect after surgery, including:

  • When you can return to work
  • How long you should avoid swimming, eye makeup, or strenuous exercise
  • What eye drops you'll need during recovery
  • How many follow-up appointments are included

Knowing the recovery timeline in advance makes it easier to plan around work, travel, and other commitments while giving your eyes the best opportunity to heal.

5. How much experience do you have performing LASIK?

Experience matters when it comes to any surgical procedure. Don't hesitate to ask about our surgeons’ training, qualifications, and history performing LASIK.

Helpful questions include:

  • How many LASIK procedures have you performed?
  • Are you board certified?
  • How do you handle unexpected findings during surgery?
  • What is your approach if additional treatment is needed later?

Our experienced LASIK surgeons understand that every eye presents unique characteristics. Their expertise allows them to recognize subtle factors that influence treatment planning and long-term visual outcomes.

The right questions lead to greater confidence

LASIK is more than a procedure. It's a decision that can have a lasting impact on your daily life. Taking time to ask thoughtful questions during your consultation helps you better understand your options while building trust with your surgeon.

We never want your LASIK consultation to feel rushed. Instead, it should leave you with clear answers, realistic expectations, and confidence that your surgeon is recommending the treatment that's truly best for your vision.

title: LASIK and Your Prescription: How Stable Does Your Vision Need to Be?
desc: Not everyone is an immediate candidate for LASIK. In fact, prescription stability is one of the most important factors we consider before recommending it. Here�
html:
LASIK has helped millions of people by offering clearer vision and greater convenience without the need for prescription glasses or contact lenses. However, if your vision is still changing, undergoing LASIK too soon may affect the treatment's long-term success.

LASIK is one of our specialties at Marano Eye Care, a division of Ophthalmology New Jersey. Because we’re committed to successful outcomes, we consider several factors before recommending this very popular procedure.

Here’s a basic look at why prescription stability matters so much and how we assess whether your vision is ready for LASIK.

Why prescription stability matters with LASIK

LASIK works by reshaping the cornea to correct refractive errors such as nearsightedness (myopia), farsightedness (hyperopia), and astigmatism. The procedure is designed to match your current prescription. Thus, if your vision continues to change after surgery, the correction may no longer align with your visual needs.

For example, if your prescription becomes stronger after LASIK, you may experience blurry vision again and require glasses, contact lenses, or an enhancement procedure. Stable vision helps ensure that the results of LASIK remain effective for as long as possible.

What is considered a stable prescription?

We typically recommend that your prescription remain relatively unchanged for at least one year before LASIK. In general, a change of less than 0.50 diopters during that period is considered stable.

Your Marano Eye Care provider will compare records from recent eye exams to determine whether your vision has remained consistent. If significant changes are detected, you may be advised to wait before moving forward with surgery.

Factors that can cause vision changes

Several factors can contribute to fluctuations in your prescription. Age is one of the most common reasons. Younger individuals, especially teenagers and people in their early 20s, may still experience natural vision changes as their eyes continue to develop.

Other factors include hormonal changes, pregnancy, certain medications, uncontrolled diabetes, and eye conditions that affect the shape of the cornea. Addressing these underlying issues can help create a more predictable outcome if LASIK is performed later.

How eye surgeons evaluate prescription stability for LASIK

During a LASIK consultation, your Marano Eye Care provider conducts a comprehensive eye examination. This includes measuring your current prescription, assessing corneal thickness, evaluating eye health, and reviewing your vision history.

Past prescriptions provide valuable insight into whether your eyesight has remained stable over time. In some cases, your surgeon may request records from previous eye exams to confirm that your prescription has not changed significantly.

What if your prescription is still changing?

If your prescription isn’t yet stable, patience is often the best approach. Waiting until your vision settles can improve the likelihood of long-lasting results and reduce the need for future corrective procedures.

Regular eye exams can help monitor changes and determine when you may become a suitable candidate for LASIK. While delaying surgery may feel disappointing, it can ultimately lead to better visual outcomes.

Wondering if you’re ready for LASIK?

Prescription stability is a key requirement for successful LASIK surgery, but you’ll never know if your eyes are ready unless you check.

By ensuring your vision has stabilized, we can maximize the chances of achieving clear, lasting results so you can enjoy the full benefits of LASIK for years to come.

title: Common LASIK Myths: What Eye Surgeons Want You to Know
desc: Fear of pain, concerns about safety, and confusion about recovery often prevent people from exploring a treatment that could improve their vision and quality of
html:
Modern LASIK technology is highly advanced, precise, and widely trusted by eye surgeons worldwide, including here at Marano Eye Care, a division of Ophthalmology New Jersey, in Denville, Livingston, and Newark, New Jersey.

Despite its success record, many myths still exist about LASIK. We hope that understanding the facts behind the most common misconceptions will help you make informed decisions with confidence.

Here are five LASIK myths our team often hears, along with the truth about this very advanced eye surgery.

Myth 1: LASIK is painful

One of the most common fears about LASIK is that the surgery is extremely painful. In reality, most people report only mild pressure during the procedure and little to no pain afterward.

To achieve that, we use numbing eye drops before surgery, making the process comfortable for the patient. The actual procedure usually takes less than 15 minutes for both eyes, and the laser portion only lasts a few seconds.

Some people experience temporary dryness or mild irritation after surgery, but this typically improves within 24-48 hours. In fact, most of our patients are pleasantly surprised by how quick and easy the experience feels.

Myth 2: LASIK can cause blindness

Many people worry that LASIK is dangerous or could lead to blindness. In fact, LASIK is considered one of the safest elective procedures available today.

Serious complications are extremely rare when a qualified and experienced surgeon performs the procedure. Advanced laser technology allows us to customize treatment for each patient’s eyes with remarkable accuracy.

In addition, we use modern screening methods to help determine whether a person is a good candidate before the surgery even begins. Patients with certain eye conditions, such as severe dry eye, may not qualify. This step further improves overall safety outcomes.

Myth 3: LASIK results don’t last

Some believe LASIK only provides temporary results. The truth is that LASIK permanently reshapes the cornea to correct vision problems such as nearsightedness (myopia), farsightedness (hyperopia), and astigmatism. For most patients, the improvement is long-lasting.

However, LASIK can’t stop natural aging changes in the eyes. For example, many adults eventually develop presbyopia, an age-related condition that affects near vision after age 40. This is a normal part of aging and not a sign that LASIK failed.

However, while your vision may change slightly over time, the original LASIK correction itself remains effective.

Myth 4: Everyone can have LASIK

LASIK is highly effective, but it is not suitable for everyone. A proper consultation is essential to determine your eligibility.

At Marano Eye Care, we evaluate several factors, including corneal thickness, prescription stability, overall eye health, and medical history. Certain conditions, such as severe dry eye, uncontrolled diabetes, or specific corneal disorders, may make LASIK unsuitable for some patients.

Fortunately, alternative vision correction procedures are available for individuals who aren’t ideal candidates for LASIK. We consider honest evaluations and personalized recommendations key components of responsible eye care.

Myth 5: Recovery takes a long time

Another common misconception is that LASIK requires weeks of recovery. In fact, most patients notice improved vision within 24 hours.

Many people return to work and routine activities within a day or two. However, we typically recommend you avoid swimming, heavy exercise, or eye makeup for a short period.

Carefully following postoperative instructions plays an important role in healing. Patients are usually given medicated eye drops and advised to attend follow-up appointments to monitor progress.

Overall, the LASIK recovery process is generally fast, smooth, and far easier than many people expect.

Need to know more about LASIK?

title: When Is the Best Time to Get LASIK? Age, Lifestyle, and Vision Stability Explained
desc: Laser vision correction has helped millions reduce or eliminate their dependence on glasses and contact lenses. But when is the right time to get LASIK? It depe
html:
The answer about when to move forward with LASIK (laser-assisted in situ keratomileusis) isn’t as simple as picking a date on the calendar. Instead, it depends on a combination of factors, especially your age, daily habits, and the stability of your vision over time.

Our team at Marano Eye Care, a division of Ophthalmology New Jersey, develops personalized treatment strategies to meet your eye care needs. This means we consider all pertinent factors when recommending various procedures, such as LASIK.

Understanding these elements can help you decide whether now is the ideal moment to move forward.

Age and why it matters

Age plays a significant role in determining LASIK eligibility. We recommend waiting until at least 18 years old. However, many patients benefit from waiting until their early to mid-20s. This is because vision can continue to change during the late teen years.

For adults in their 20s and 30s, LASIK tends to offer the most predictable and long-lasting results. During this period, prescriptions are more likely to stabilize, making it easier to achieve accurate correction.

If you’re in your 40s or older, LASIK can still be a great option, but there’s an added consideration: presbyopia. This natural, age-related condition affects near vision and may still require reading glasses after surgery. While LASIK can effectively correct distance vision, it doesn’t stop the aging process of the eye.

Vision stability required

As noted, one of the most important factors in determining the right time for LASIK is vision stability. We typically look for a consistent prescription for at least one to two years before approving surgery.

Why does this matter? If your vision is still changing, the results of LASIK may not last as long as expected. If your prescription continues to worsen after surgery, you could eventually need glasses again.

Signs your vision may be stable include:

  • No significant changes in your prescription during recent eye exams
  • Consistent clarity with your current corrective lenses
  • No ongoing eye health issues affecting your sight

If your vision fluctuates frequently, it’s usually best to wait until it settles. We can help you make this decision based on your previous and current eye exams.

Matching LASIK to your lifestyle

Your lifestyle can strongly influence whether it’s the right time for LASIK. People with active routines often benefit the most from the procedure.

If you play sports, swim regularly, or work in environments where glasses or contacts are inconvenient, LASIK can provide a noticeable improvement in comfort and convenience. Similarly, individuals with demanding schedules may appreciate not having to manage contact lens care.

However, timing still matters. For instance, if you’re planning a major life event, such as a wedding, travel, or a busy work period, you’ll want to schedule LASIK when you can allow time for recovery.

While healing is typically quick, giving yourself a few days to rest and attend follow-up appointments is essential.

Health and eye conditions

Beyond age and lifestyle, your overall eye health must be suitable for LASIK. Conditions like dry eye syndrome, thin corneas, or certain medical issues can affect candidacy.

Pregnancy and breastfeeding can also temporarily change vision due to hormonal shifts. In these cases, doctors often recommend waiting until hormone levels stabilize before considering surgery.

A comprehensive eye exam is the only way to determine whether your eyes are healthy enough for the procedure.

So, when is the best time for LASIK?

The ideal time to get LASIK is when three key factors align: you’re an appropriate age, your vision has been stable, and your lifestyle supports both the procedure and recovery.

For many people, this sweet spot falls in their mid-20s to late 30s, but it can vary widely depending on individual circumstances. The best approach is to consult with an eye care professional who can evaluate your specific situation.

Ready to learn more about LASIK?

When the timing is right, LASIK can be a life-changing investment in both convenience and clarity. Schedule an evaluation at Marano Eye Care today by calling one of our state-of-the-art facilities in Denville, Livingston, or Newark, New Jersey.

title: LASIK vs. Other Vision Correction Options: How to Choose the Best Fit for Your Eyes
desc: Understanding the differences between LASIK and other vision correction methods can help you make an informed decision tailored to your eye health, lifestyle, a
html:
Advances in ophthalmology have made long-term vision correction more accessible than ever, with LASIK often leading the conversation. However, LASIK is not the only option available, and it may not be the best fit for everyone.

Our team at Marano Eye Care, a division of Ophthalmology New Jersey, personalizes your eye care to fit your unique needs. Here’s a look at the most common options to help you determine the right path toward clearer vision.

Defining LASIK

LASIK (laser-assisted in situ keratomileusis) is a popular refractive surgery designed to correct nearsightedness (myopia), farsightedness (hyperopia), and astigmatism.

The procedure reshapes the cornea using a precise laser, allowing light entering the eye to focus properly on the retina. LASIK is known for its quick recovery time, minimal discomfort, and high success rates. Many patients experience significantly improved vision within 24-48 hours.

However, LASIK is not suitable for everyone. Ideal candidates typically have stable vision, healthy corneas, and no underlying eye conditions such as severe dry eye or corneal disease.

PRK, a trusted alternative

Photorefractive keratectomy (PRK) is another laser vision correction procedure. Like LASIK, it reshapes the cornea, but instead of creating a flap, PRK removes the outer layer of the cornea entirely before applying the laser.

This technique can make PRK a better option for patients with thinner corneas or those at higher risk of eye trauma, such as athletes. The trade-off is a longer recovery period.

With PRK, vision improvement may take several days to weeks, and patients may experience more discomfort during healing. Despite this, PRK delivers results comparable to LASIK.

Implantable collamer lenses (ICL)

For patients who aren’t candidates for laser surgery, implantable collamer lenses offer an effective alternative. In this procedure, a biocompatible lens is inserted into the eye without removing the natural lens.

ICL is especially beneficial for individuals with high prescriptions or thin corneas. One advantage of ICL is that it’s reversible and doesn’t permanently alter the cornea.

However, ICL is a more invasive procedure than LASIK or PRK and may involve a longer recovery and higher cost.

Refractive lens exchange (RLE)

Refractive lens exchange is similar to cataract surgery and involves replacing the eye’s natural lens with an artificial intraocular lens (IOL). This option is often recommended for patients over 40 who may also be experiencing presbyopia, or age-related difficulty focusing on close objects.

RLE can correct a wide range of vision issues and eliminate the need for reading glasses in many cases. Because it is an intraocular procedure, it carries more risk than laser-based surgeries but can provide long-lasting results.

Glasses and contact lenses

Nonsurgical options like glasses and contact lenses remain popular methods of vision correction. They are safe, accessible, and require no recovery time. Additionally, advances in lens technology have significantly improved comfort and visual clarity.

However, these options require ongoing maintenance and costs over time.

Choosing the best option

Choosing the best vision correction method depends on several factors, including your prescription, corneal thickness, age, lifestyle, and overall eye health.

For instance, someone with an active lifestyle may prefer a long-term surgical solution, while others may prioritize flexibility and opt for nonsurgical methods.

At Marano Eye Care, we start with a comprehensive eye examination, which is essential to determine candidacy for each procedure. During the consultation, your ophthalmologist will evaluate your eyes and discuss your goals to recommend the most appropriate option.

Take the next step

There is no one-size-fits-all solution when it comes to vision correction. While LASIK is a highly effective and popular choice, alternatives like PRK, ICL, and RLE offer valuable options for patients with different needs.

Schedule an appointment today at our offices in Denville, Livingston, or Newark, New Jersey, for expert guidance regarding your best options for clear, comfortable vision.

title: Life After LASIK: What Patients Can Expect During Recovery and Beyond
desc: LASIK has transformed the way we approach refractive errors, offering a safe and effective way to achieve clearer vision without relying on corrective eyewear.
html:
For millions of people, glasses and contact lenses are part of daily life. If you prefer life without corrective lenses, LASIK (laser-assisted in situ keratomileusis) may be an excellent alternative.

But what happens afterward? How long does it take your eyes to heal? Are the changes permanent?

LASIK is one of our specialties at Marano Eye Care, a division of Ophthalmology New Jersey, with offices in Denville, Livingston, and Newark. We use the most advanced technology and treatments available to improve and preserve vision.

We also find that sometimes the most effective tool we have is communicating with our patients about what to expect before, during, and after a procedure.  

While every case is different and results can vary, we’re happy to provide basic information about what you can expect after LASIK.

The first 24 hours

Most patients are pleasantly surprised by how quickly they notice an improvement in vision. Within just a few hours after LASIK, vision often becomes significantly clearer, though it may still appear slightly hazy or fluctuate as healing occurs.

Common sensations during the first day include:

  • Mild burning or stinging
  • Mild itchiness
  • Light sensitivity
  • Excess tearing

These symptoms are normal and typically resolve within 24-48 hours. We advise patients to rest their eyes, keep them closed as much as possible, and avoid screens on the day of surgery.

Protective eye shields should be worn while sleeping to prevent accidental rubbing.

The first week

During the first week, vision continues to sharpen and stabilize. Many patients return to work within one to three days, depending on their occupation.

Driving is often possible within a day or two, once vision meets legal standards. However, some temporary visual effects may occur:

  • Halos around lights
  • Glare at night
  • Fluctuating clarity
  • Mild dryness

Dry eye symptoms are especially common. The corneal nerves, which help regulate tear production, need time to regenerate. We prescribe eyedrops several times daily to maintain comfort and promote healing.

Follow-up visits, starting with a recheck two to three days after the procedure, are essential during this period. We encourage you to schedule and keep every appointment and follow postsurgical care instructions carefully to ensure proper healing and optimal visual outcomes.

The first month

By the one-month mark, most patients experience stable, crisp vision. Activities such as exercising, swimming (after approval), and wearing eye makeup can usually resume without restriction.

Dryness may persist in some individuals, particularly those with preexisting dry eye symptoms. Consistent use of lubricating drops and, in some cases, prescription treatments can help manage this phase.

Please do not use drops or other eye medications without express approval from your eye surgeon.

Night vision disturbances, such as halos or starbursts, generally diminish over time as the brain adapts to the new visual system. This neuroadaptation is a normal process and can take several weeks.

What to expect beyond recovery

LASIK corrects refractive errors such as nearsightedness (myopia), farsightedness (hyperopia), and astigmatism by permanently reshaping the cornea. For the vast majority of patients, results are long-lasting and stable.

However, it’s important to understand that LASIK does not prevent natural age-related changes. For instance, around age 40 and beyond, many individuals develop presbyopia, a normal condition that affects near vision.

Even patients with excellent LASIK outcomes may eventually need reading glasses to correct presbyopia.

Additionally, although LASIK reduces dependence on glasses or contacts, it does not eliminate the need for regular comprehensive eye exams. 

Routine evaluations help monitor overall ocular health, detect conditions such as glaucoma or macular degeneration, and ensure lasting visual clarity.

Ready for the freedom offered by LASIK?

One of the most rewarding aspects of LASIK is the freedom it provides in your daily life. Patients often describe simple pleasures, such as waking up and seeing clearly, swimming without contacts, or traveling without spare lenses, as transformative.

title: Is LASIK Right for You? What Eye Surgeons Evaluate Before Recommending Surgery
desc: While LASIK can be life-changing, it’s not a one-size-fits-all solution. Before recommending surgery, eye surgeons carefully consider several factors, ranging
html:
For many, the benefits of LASIK are hard to resist. It’s an advanced procedure that has helped millions of people eliminate the need for glasses and contact lenses.

However, while satisfaction rates are high, LASIK isn’t appropriate for everyone. That’s why our team at Marano Eye Care, a division of Ophthalmology New Jersey, carefully evaluates your current eye health and medical history before recommending LASIK.

What eye surgeons evaluate before recommending LASIK

Here are key factors our team considers when helping you decide whether LASIK is right for you:

1. Your prescription and vision stability

One of the first things we check is whether your vision prescription has been stable for at least 12 months. LASIK works best when nearsightedness, farsightedness, or astigmatism is no longer changing.

If your prescription is still shifting, surgery may be postponed to avoid under- or overcorrection later. We also confirm whether your prescription falls within safe treatment ranges established through clinical research and outcomes.

2. Corneal thickness and shape

LASIK reshapes the cornea to improve how light focuses on the retina. To do this safely, your corneas must be thick and strong enough. Advanced imaging and mapping technology allow our eye surgeons to measure corneal thickness and detect irregularities.

If the cornea is too thin or has an abnormal shape, LASIK may not be recommended. However, your Marano Eye Care surgeon may suggest an alternative procedure in this case.

3. Overall eye health

Healthy eyes are essential for successful LASIK outcomes. During your evaluation, surgeons look for conditions such as chronic dry eye, corneal disease, glaucoma, or retinal problems.

Some health issues, such as poorly managed diabetes, may at least temporarily disqualify you. This thorough screening helps protect your long-term vision and reduces the risk of complications.

4. Pupil size and night vision risk

Pupil size, especially in low-light conditions, plays a role in LASIK candidacy. Larger pupils can increase the risk of post-surgery night vision symptoms, such as halos or glare. Modern laser technology has significantly reduced these risks, but surgeons still evaluate pupil size to personalize treatment and set realistic expectations.

5. Age and vision changes

Most surgeons recommend LASIK for adults over 18 whose eyes have fully developed. Age also matters later in life. For instance, people over 40 may develop presbyopia, a natural age-related loss of near vision.

While LASIK can correct distance vision, it doesn’t stop age-related changes. Thus, your surgeon will discuss whether you may still need reading glasses in the future.

6. Lifestyle and visual goals

Your daily activities matter. Athletes, frequent travelers, and people in physically demanding jobs often benefit significantly from LASIK. Your surgeon also asks about hobbies, screen time, and night driving habits to ensure the procedure aligns with your lifestyle and expectations.

7. Expectations and safety considerations

At Marano Eye Care, we also consider whether your expectations are realistic. LASIK aims to reduce dependence on glasses or contacts significantly, but it does not guarantee “perfect” vision for everyone.

Our goal is to provide clear information about LASIK that offers an understanding of the benefits and limitations, and prioritizes safety over speed or convenience. That said, LASIK is often an excellent alternative to glasses or contacts and certainly deserves its reputation for efficacy and high patient satisfaction.

Want to learn more about LASIK?

We start with a comprehensive evaluation that ensures the procedure is safe, effective, and tailored to your eyes.

title: 3 Early Signs of Macular Degeneration You Shouldn't Ignore
desc: Macular degeneration is one of the leading causes of vision loss, especially in adults over 50. Recognizing the early signs of macular degeneration is critical
html:
Macular degeneration is usually age-related and affects the macula, the part of your retina responsible for sharp, central vision. Daily activities like driving, reading, and recognizing a loved one's face all depend on central vision.

Because symptoms of age-related macular degeneration (AMD) often develop gradually, many people ignore early warning signs until vision loss becomes noticeable. There is no cure (yet) for AMD, but there is much we can do to help slow its progression.

Therefore, when it comes to AMD, one of our goals at Marano Eye Care, a division of Ophthalmology New Jersey, is to detect changes in the macula early, sometimes even before vision loss occurs.

We can do this during comprehensive eye exams by using a special lens to view the retina and advanced technology to capture detailed images of the back of the eye.

You can also help by being aware of three early symptoms of AMD you should never ignore.

1. Blurry or distorted central vision

One of the earliest and most common signs of macular degeneration is changes in central vision. You may notice that objects directly in front of you appear blurry, distorted, or less sharp than usual.

Straight lines, such as door frames or text on a page, may begin to look wavy or bent, a symptom known as metamorphopsia. This change often makes everyday tasks like reading, driving, or recognizing faces more difficult.

Because peripheral (side) vision remains intact when you have AMD, you may assume the blurriness is minor or due to eye strain. However, persistent central vision distortion should never be ignored, as it can signal early-stage AMD.

The Amsler grid is an easy check for possible AMD-related visual disturbances you can try at home. Available for online printing, this chart features a grid-like pattern with a dot at the center. Focusing on the dot while covering one eye, then the other, can help identify issues in central vision.

2. Difficulty seeing in low light

Another early sign of macular degeneration is difficulty adjusting to low-light conditions. You may find it harder to see clearly in dim settings, such as restaurants or at night. Tasks like reading menus in low light or driving after sunset can become more difficult.

This symptom happens because the macula is essential for adjusting vision between bright and dark conditions. If your eyes take longer than usual to adapt when switching from bright light to darkness, it may signal early retinal changes.

3. Colors appearing dull or less vibrant

Changes in color perception can also be an early warning sign of macular degeneration. Colors may appear faded, dull, or less vibrant than before, particularly reds and greens.

This happens because the macula contains cells that detect fine details and color contrast. You may not notice this change immediately, but over time, everyday objects may seem less vivid.

If you find yourself increasing screen brightness or struggling to distinguish between similar shades, it could be related to early macular damage.

What’s the next step?

Early detection of macular degeneration is essential because treatments are most effective before significant vision loss occurs. While there is no cure for AMD, lifestyle changes, nutritional supplements, and medical treatments can slow its progression.

However, visual disturbances related to AMD are often subtle and difficult to pinpoint at first. Therefore, regular comprehensive eye exams, especially after age 50, are crucial for detecting early changes in the macula.

title: Start the New Year with Clear Vision: Is a PanOptix® Lens Right for You?

The PanOptix® intraocular lens (IOL) is designed to provide crisp, seamless vision at near, intermediate, and far distances.

It’s one of the advanced lens options our surgeons at Marano Eye Care, a division of Ophthalmology New Jersey, may recommend for individuals undergoing cataract surgery.

Here’s more from our team about how the PanOptix® lens works, who makes an ideal candidate, and what benefits you can expect. If you’re considering vision correction in the new year, this guide is a great place to start.

Intraocular lens basics

Cataracts occur when the eye’s natural lens becomes clouded, resulting in blurry and distorted vision that worsens as the clouding progresses.

During cataract surgery, your provider replaces the clouded lens with an artificial intraocular lens implant. This removes the visual distortions and overcomes vision loss caused by cataracts.

There are several types of IOLs available, including those that can correct refractive errors, such as nearsightedness or astigmatism.

What makes the PanOptix lens different?

While all types of IOLs can clear the cloudiness caused by cataracts, not all can address multiple issues. For instance, a monofocal IOL clears the cataract and can be set for distance vision, but you may require glasses for reading or other close work.

On the other hand, the PanOptix IOL is a trifocal lens engineered using cutting-edge technology, providing crisp vision at near, intermediate, and far distances. This can eliminate the need for additional glasses or contact lenses to correct common issues like presbyopia.

The enhanced intermediate vision available with the PanOptix lens improves your ability to use digital devices or view dashboards, activities that are a large part of modern life. Thus, whether you’re reading, using a computer, or driving, PanOptix can optimize your vision following cataract surgery.

Who is a good candidate for PanOptix?

Your Marano Eye Care provider may recommend PanOptix if you:

  • Want greater independence from reading or computer glasses
  • Struggle with a combination of refractive errors (i.e., nearsightedness and presbyopia)
  • Lead an active lifestyle and frequently switch between visual tasks
  • Have healthy eyes aside from cataracts

However, the PanOptix lens may not be the best choice for individuals with certain eye conditions such as significant macular degeneration, severe dry eye, or advanced glaucoma.

Our providers recommend IOL types based on a comprehensive eye exam and personalized consultation to determine the best option for your vision goals.

What results can I expect with PanOptix?

Most patients enjoy clearer vision almost immediately after surgery, with continued improvement as the eyes heal. You can also expect minimal dependence on glasses, even for tasks such as reading or detailed work.

title: Can Your Cataracts Come Back After Cataract Surgery?
desc: Have you noticed a haze or fogginess to your vision that reminds you of what it felt like before your cataract surgery? Does that mean cataracts can return afte
html:
Cataract surgery is one of the most common and successful eye procedures performed today. It restores clear vision for millions of people each year. And once a cataract is removed, it can’t return.

However, there’s a condition that can cause vision to become cloudy again, which sometimes leads people to believe their cataract has come back.

Our team at Marano Eye Care, a division of Ophthalmology New Jersey, can clear up some of the confusion about whether cataracts can return.

Understanding cataracts

If you’ve had or are contemplating surgery, you likely know by now that cataracts occur when the natural lens of your eye becomes cloudy, usually due to aging. This cloudiness blocks light and makes it difficult to see clearly.

During cataract surgery, your ophthalmologist removes the cloudy lens and replaces it with a clear, artificial lens called an intraocular lens (IOL). Since the natural lens is permanently replaced, a cataract itself can’t grow back.

So why does vision sometimes get cloudy again?

Months or even years after surgery, some patients experience blurred or hazy vision that feels similar to having cataracts again. This is usually caused by a condition called posterior capsule opacification (PCO), often referred to as a secondary cataract.

During cataract surgery, your surgeon leaves the thin, transparent membrane (posterior lens capsule) that holds your new lens in place. Over time, this capsule can become cloudy due to cell growth.

When this happens, light can’t pass through the lens as clearly, making your vision appear foggy again. Thus, while the cataract hasn’t returned, you may be experiencing some of the same symptoms.

Treating posterior capsule opacification

The good news is that PCO is quick and easy to fix with a procedure called laser capsulotomy. It’s painless, takes only a few minutes, and doesn’t require any incisions or downtime.

The laser creates a small opening in the cloudy capsule, allowing light to pass through clearly again. Most patients notice an immediate improvement in vision.

Preventing future cloudiness

While PCO can’t always be prevented, newer lens technologies and surgical techniques have reduced how often it occurs.

The Marano Eye Care team recommends that you have regular eye exams after cataract surgery to help your ophthalmologist monitor your eye health and detect any changes early.

Struggling with hazy vision or worried about a worsening cataract?

title: What Is Corneal Cross-Linking and How Does It Help Keratoconus?
desc: If you or a loved one has been diagnosed with keratoconus, you may have heard about a treatment called corneal cross-linking (CXL). Read why our specialty team
html:
Corneal cross-linking (CXL) is an innovative procedure that’s changing the way ophthalmologists manage keratoconus. It offers patients hope for better vision and long-term stability.

Diagnosing and treating keratoconus is one of our specialties at Marano Eye Care, a division of Ophthalmology New Jersey. Let’s take a closer look at what corneal cross-linking is, how it works, and why it can make a difference.

Understanding keratoconus

Keratoconus affects the cornea, the clear, dome-shaped surface at the front of the eye. In healthy eyes, the cornea holds a regular, round shape that helps focus light onto the retina for clear vision.

In keratoconus, the cornea gradually thins and bulges outward into a cone-like shape. This distortion causes blurry vision, increased sensitivity to light, and frequent adjustments to prescription glasses or contact lenses.

While mild keratoconus can sometimes be managed with specialty contact lenses, progressive cases can lead to significant vision problems and eventually require a corneal transplant.

Our treatment goal for keratoconus is to prevent progression while improving your vision.

What is corneal cross-linking?

Corneal cross-linking is a minimally invasive outpatient procedure designed to strengthen the cornea and stop keratoconus from worsening.

It works by creating new "cross-links" between the collagen fibers in the cornea, similar to adding extra support beams to a weak structure.

The treatment involves two main steps:

  1. Applying riboflavin (vitamin B2) eye drops to the cornea
  2. Exposing the cornea to controlled ultraviolet (UV) light, which activates the riboflavin and strengthens the corneal tissue

This process increases the cornea’s stability, making it more resistant to further bulging or thinning.

Benefits of corneal cross-linking

The most significant benefit of corneal cross-linking is that it can halt or slow the progression of keratoconus. CXL won’t correct your vision, but it helps preserve your current level of sight and prevents further deterioration.

Our team then prescribes contact lenses, eyeglasses, or other therapies to correct the blurry vision and other issues related to pretreatment keratoconus.

Other benefits of CXL include:

Reducing the need for corneal transplant

By stabilizing the cornea early, many individuals can avoid more invasive surgeries later.

Improved contact lens tolerance

With a stronger cornea, many patients find contact lenses more comfortable and effective.

Long-term results

Studies show that corneal cross-linking provides lasting stabilization for most patients.

Who is a good candidate for corneal cross-linking?

Corneal cross-linking is most effective for individuals diagnosed with progressive keratoconus or other corneal weakening conditions. Our team usually recommends treatment when changes in vision, prescription, or corneal scans show that the condition is worsening.

Keratoconus usually develops in older teens and young adults. Because timing is critical, early diagnosis is key. The sooner keratoconus is detected, the better the chance of preserving your vision with cross-linking.

Routine eye exams are essential for diagnosing and treating keratoconus, especially following therapies like CXL.

What to expect during and after the procedure

The procedure typically takes about an hour. You’re awake, but we use numbing drops to ensure comfort.

After treatment, your eyes may feel irritated or sensitive for one to two days. Most people can return to normal activities within a week, and follow-up visits help monitor progress.

title: My Floaters Are Driving Me Crazy. What Are My Treatment Options?
desc: Eye floaters are usually harmless, until they’re not. Learn more about treatment options for these dots, circles, and squiggly lines that drift lazily across
html:
Floaters are so common that it would be strange if you didn’t develop a few during your lifetime. They’re especially noticeable when you’re looking at a bright background like a clear sky or white wall.

Most often harmless and related to the natural aging process, floaters can become incredibly distracting. And, in some cases, a sudden increase could indicate an underlying disorder that requires immediate medical care.

The team at Marano Eye Care, a division of Ophthalmology New Jersey, offers outstanding eye care services to adults and teens from our offices in Denville, Livingston, and Newark, New Jersey.

Our expertise includes diagnosing and treating, when necessary, the underlying cause of floaters. Here’s more from our team regarding what floaters are, when you should be concerned, and what treatment options are available.

What exactly are floaters?

Floaters occur when tiny clumps of collagen form in the vitreous. This is the clear, gel-like substance that fills the inside of your eye. When light passes through the eye, these clumps cast shadows on the retina, creating the floating shapes you see.

Most floaters are related to natural aging of the eye, but they can also appear due to:

  • Nearsightedness (myopia)
  • Eye injury
  • Previous eye surgery
  • Retinal tears or detachments
  • Inflammation at the back of the eye (posterior uveitis)

Diabetes, high blood pressure (hypertension), and blocked blood vessels can also cause bleeding into the vitreous. The resulting blood cells may be mistaken for collagen-based floaters.

When to see an ophthalmologist

We encourage everyone to have routine eye exams. This allows us to discuss changes in your vision, such as increased floaters, as we measure your visual acuity and track your eye health.

Conditions such as posterior uveitis require a specialist’s care. A sudden shower of floaters, especially when accompanied by flashes of light or a curtain-like shadow across your vision, could signal a retinal tear or detachment. This is a sight-threatening emergency that requires urgent medical care.

Otherwise, some people consider eye floaters an occasional nuisance that’s easy to ignore. For others, they interfere with activities like reading, driving, or even simply enjoying a sunny day.

If floaters are distracting you from your daily routine, we encourage you to schedule an eye exam.

Treatment options for floaters

Depending on the underlying cause, here are treatment options our Marano Eye Care specialists may discuss with you:

Observation (watchful waiting)

In many cases, floaters fade or become less noticeable over time. The brain gradually adapts and learns to ignore them.

If floaters aren’t significantly interfering with your vision, your provider may recommend monitoring the situation rather than pursuing active treatment.

Laser treatment

This minimally invasive procedure uses a medical laser to break up large floaters into smaller, less noticeable fragments. It can be an effective option for some patients, especially those with a few prominent floaters.

Vitrectomy 

For patients whose floaters are truly debilitating, your specialist may consider a vitrectomy. During this surgical procedure, which is reserved for the most severe cases, the vitreous gel (along with the floaters) is removed and replaced with a clear solution.

Finding the right solution for you

Every patient’s needs are unique. The best way to decide on treatment is through a comprehensive eye exam. Your ophthalmologist can evaluate your floaters and discuss the safest options for your situation.

If floaters are interfering with your daily life, don’t suffer in silence. Schedule an appointment at Marano Eye Care today by calling one of our New Jersey offices.

title: Does LASIK Last Forever?
desc: LASIK eye surgery has helped millions of people eliminate the need for glasses and contact lenses. It’s a quick and effective procedure and comes with a relat
html:
LASIK is a proven and effective method for improving your vision in the long term. However, while the structural results last forever, that doesn’t mean your vision won’t change.

So, what does that mean? Will it last forever or not?

Our award-winning surgeons at Marano Eye Care, a division of Ophthalmology New Jersey, can answer those questions. Check these facts from our team about LASIK and how long you can expect it to last.

LASIK basics

LASIK (laser-assisted in situ keratomileusis) is a type of eye surgery that corrects common vision problems like nearsightedness (myopia), farsightedness (hyperopia), and astigmatism.

During the procedure, your Marano Eye Care surgeon reshapes the cornea using a laser so that light entering the eye correctly focuses onto the retina. This improves your vision and often eliminates the need for corrective lenses, such as glasses or contacts.

The long-term outlook

For most people, LASIK results are long-lasting. Once your cornea is reshaped, it tends to stay that way. Studies show that 90% of patients maintain 20/20 vision or better, even 10 years after the procedure.

Researchers also believe that as the medical technology required for LASIK has improved since its inception, the safety and efficacy of the procedure continue to increase.

That said, it’s important to understand that your eyes, like the rest of your body, change with age.

How does vision change over time?

While the structural changes from LASIK are permanent, your overall eye health can still evolve over time.

Here are a few common changes that might affect your vision after LASIK:

Presbyopia (age-related focus loss)

Most people over 40 develop presbyopia, a condition that makes it harder to see things up close. This happens even if you’ve had LASIK. It’s not a failure of the surgery, just a normal part of aging. You may still need reading glasses later in life.

Natural vision changes

For a small number of people, their vision prescription might slowly shift again over time. This isn’t common, but it can happen, especially if your refractive error was very significant or unstable before LASIK.

Your eye surgeon discusses the details of a LASIK procedure, including expected outcomes, before scheduling the surgery.

Cataracts

As you age, you may develop cataracts, a condition characterized by the clouding of the lens inside your eye. LASIK doesn’t prevent this, and cataract surgery may be necessary later on.

Fortunately, having LASIK in the past doesn't usually complicate future cataract treatment.

Can you have LASIK more than once?

Yes, in some cases. If your vision changes significantly years after your first LASIK procedure, you may be eligible for a touch-up or enhancement surgery.

This is often possible if there’s enough corneal tissue left to safely reshape. At that point, your Marano Eye Care surgeon will assess whether it’s a good idea based on your eye health and vision needs.

So, does LASIK last forever?

Technically, yes, the changes to your cornea are permanent. But your vision may still evolve with age.

LASIK is not a guarantee that you’ll never need glasses again, but for many people, it means years, even decades, of sharper, glasses-free vision.

title: My Mom Has Macular Cysts, Will I Get Them Too?
desc: Genetics may play a role in the development of macular cysts. However, having a parent with macular cysts doesn’t guarantee you’ll get them too. Still, it�
html:
When a loved one develops an eye condition, especially something involving vision loss, it's natural to wonder about your own risk.

The team at Marano Eye Care focuses on protecting our patients’ vision for a lifetime. We have the expertise to provide comprehensive eye care, ranging from maintaining visual acuity with the latest in corrective lenses and surgery to advanced treatments for conditions such as macular cysts.

We’re also dedicated to keeping our patients informed about their eye health and taking a proactive approach to conditions that can affect vision. Here’s what we want you to know about macular cysts and genetics.

What are macular cysts?

The macula is a small, round area at the center of the retina. It’s responsible for sharp central vision, which is necessary for activities such as driving, recognizing faces, and reading.

Macular cysts (also commonly referred to as macular holes) are tiny openings that develop in the macula, causing blurred vision or other visual distortions (i.e., wavy lines).

What causes macular cysts?

There are several causes, and they vary widely, including:

  • Previous eye surgery
  • Diabetes
  • Retinal vein occlusions (a kind of eye stroke)
  • Inflammatory diseases (like uveitis)
  • Certain genetic conditions
  • Eye injury

Sometimes, macular cysts can develop without a clear cause, but in many cases, they're linked to underlying health issues or structural changes in the eye.

For instance, they may show up as part of a condition called cystoid macular edema (CME), characterized by swelling in the macula due to fluid accumulation.

So, if your mom has macular cysts, are you likely to get them too?

The short answer? Not necessarily.

Most causes of macular cysts are not directly inherited. For example, if your mom developed them after cataract surgery or due to diabetes, that doesn’t mean you’ll develop the same issue, unless you share the same risk factors.

However, if her cysts are part of a genetic retinal condition (like juvenile retinoschisis or certain types of macular dystrophies), then yes, there may be a hereditary component.

However, even then, genetics is only one part of the story. Your overall risk also depends on lifestyle, general health, and age.

Can you treat macular cysts?

Yes, and often very successfully. Treatment depends on the underlying cause, size of the cyst, and how it’s affecting your vision. Here are the most common approaches:

Watchful waiting

For smaller cysts that aren’t significantly impacting vision, your Marano Eye Care provider may recommend careful monitoring through follow-up eye exams. 

Eye drops

For mild cases, especially after surgery, anti-inflammatory drops (such as steroid or NSAID drops) can help reduce swelling and aid in the resolution of the cysts.

Injections

If cysts are related to diabetes, vein occlusion, or inflammation, medications like anti-VEGF drugs (e.g., Avastin®, Eylea®) or steroids may be injected directly into the eye.

An eye injection may sound scary, but it's quick and usually painless.

Oral medications

For inflammatory causes, our team may prescribe oral medication to reduce swelling.

Surgery

Rarely, if structural issues cause cysts or don’t respond to medication, we might consider surgery to close the macular hole.

The good news is that with early detection and the right treatment plan, vision often improves or at least stabilizes.

So, what now?

If you have a family history of eye disease, the best thing you can do is stay ahead of it:

Get regular eye exams

We recommend routine eye exams for teens and adults. However, this is especially important if you’re over 40 or have health issues like diabetes or high blood pressure (hypertension).

Track your family history

Learn what you can about your family’s medical history. Then share the details with your Marano Eye Care provider. It helps us know what to look for.

Monitor changes

Blurry spots, distortion, or sudden changes? Don’t wait. Get checked.

Regular checkups, healthy habits, and early intervention go a long way in protecting your vision. Schedule a visit at Marano Eye Care today.

title: What Your Red Eyes May Be Saying About Your Health
desc: A late night or prolonged screen time can leave you with tired, red, irritated eyes. We’ve all experienced it, but if the redness persists or recurs frequentl
html:
While red eyes can be a sign of tiredness or allergies, they may also indicate infections, chronic dry eye, or more serious conditions such as glaucoma or uveitis.

Our team at Marano Eye Care can solve the riddle of what’s causing your eye redness and develop a treatment plan focused on protecting your vision.

Here are a few potential causes of red eyes and what that might mean about your eye health.

1. Lack of sleep or eye strain

If you've been burning the midnight oil or spending too much time staring at screens, your eyes may respond with redness. Fatigue reduces the amount of oxygen reaching your eyes, causing blood vessels to dilate and leading to a bloodshot appearance.

Try the 20-20-20 remedy to reduce screen strain. Look at something 20 feet away every 20 minutes for 20 seconds. It may take time for this to become a habit. Setting an alarm on your phone might help. It’s well worth the effort to give your eyes a break.

2. Allergies

Seasonal allergies or sensitivities to pet dander, dust, or pollen can trigger itchy, red, watery eyes. This happens when your immune system releases histamines in response to allergens.

Watch for sneezing, runny nose, or itchy skin along with red eyes, and check with your physician for allergy testing and treatment if you’re experiencing these symptoms.

3. Dry eyes

Dry eye occurs when your tear ducts aren’t producing enough or the correct balance of lubrication. The lack of a healthy tear layer can cause eye inflammation and redness.

Environmental issues, such as air conditioning or a windy day, can cause temporary symptoms. However, chronic dry eyes may be related to an underlying medical condition such as Sjögren’s syndrome, certain medications, or a blockage of the tiny meibomian oil glands that line the eyelids.

Chronic dry eyes can lead to blurry vision, sensitivity to light, and problems wearing contact lenses. Your Marano Eye Care specialist may recommend treatments such as prescription-strength eyedrops or a LipiFlow® procedure to clear blocked oil glands

4. Conjunctivitis

Best known as “pink eye,” bacterial or viral infections can cause conjunctivitis or be related to allergies. Symptoms include eye redness, pain, and discharge.

Eye redness accompanied by yellow/green discharge or severe discomfort requires medical attention.

5. Contact lens issues

Wearing contact lenses too long or not cleaning them properly can irritate your eyes, cause redness, and even lead to serious infections. Follow proper lens hygiene and schedule a visit if wearing your lenses as directed is causing discomfort, blurred vision, or excessive tearing.

6. Glaucoma

Red eyes and pain? Don’t ignore it. These may be signs of acute angle-closure glaucoma, a medical emergency that can lead to vision loss if untreated. Other signs include blurred vision, blind spots (scotomas), or halos around lights.

7. Uveitis

This is inflammation inside the eye that can cause redness, pain, and light sensitivity. Uveitis is often associated with autoimmune disorders, such as rheumatoid arthritis or lupus, and requires prompt medical treatment to protect your vision.

8. Subconjunctival hemorrhage

Sometimes a red eye is caused by a small blood vessel bursting, which can look alarming but is usually harmless and typically clears on its own. Causes include coughing, sneezing, or straining.

Concerned about your red eyes?

desc: Have you ever squinted at a street sign, only to see it blur into a fuzzy mess? Or do headlights at night seem stretched or distorted? You might be one of the m
html:
Astigmatism is a refractive error; it’s medical speak for “your eye doesn’t bend light the way it should.” It happens when parts of the eye are football-shaped rather than nicely curved like a basketball. 

Our team at Marano Eye Care, a division of Ophthalmology New Jersey, is well-versed in diagnosing and treating astigmatism, which may or may not require treatment.

Here’s what you need to know about astigmatism and when we recommend treatment.

Astigmatism basics

There are two types of astigmatism: corneal (affecting the cornea) and lenticular (affecting the lens).

Typically, the cornea (the clear front surface of your eye) or lens (the part inside your eye that helps focus) is curved like a basketball. When you have astigmatism, the lens or cornea is shaped more like a football or an egg.

This irregular shape prevents light from focusing correctly on the light-sensitive tissue (retina) at the back of your eye, which helps you see clearly.

Astigmatism can coexist with myopia (nearsightedness) or hyperopia (farsightedness), increasing problems with blurred or distorted vision up close and far away.

What causes astigmatism?

Astigmatism is usually something you're born with, but can also develop later in life. It might be caused by:

  • Genetics
  • Eye injuries
  • Eye surgery
  • Keratoconus (when the cornea thins and becomes cone-shaped)

Symptoms can vary, but many people are aware of a problem because of blurry vision. Astigmatism may interfere with routine tasks like reading words on a chalkboard or seeing clearly at night.

However, young children may not recognize a problem since they likely believe everyone sees the world the way they do. This makes childhood eye exams essential. Other symptoms of astigmatism include squinting, headaches, and eye discomfort/fatigue.

Treating astigmatism

Astigmatism is easily detectable on a comprehensive exam and may be mild enough that you don’t need treatment. However, routine eye exams are essential in protecting your vision, because astigmatism can worsen over time.

If you do need treatment to see clearly, there are plenty of ways to correct astigmatism:

Glasses

Glasses are the simplest and most common option for treating astigmatism. Special lenses help refocus light onto the retina, giving you clearer vision.

Contact lenses

Soft toric lenses are designed specifically for astigmatism. Some people may also benefit from rigid gas-permeable (RGP) lenses, which provide sharper vision for more severe cases.

Laser eye surgery

Procedures like LASIK or PRK can permanently reshape the cornea, correcting the irregular curve that causes astigmatism.

At Marano Eye Care, we base our recommendations on your exam results, the severity of the curvature, and its effects on your vision. You can expect a detailed discussion of the benefits vs the risks of glasses, contacts, or surgery.
